Ibn Kathir explains these as mountain passes through which people may travel from region to region and country to country. As we can see, he says, the mountains form barriers between one land and another, so Allah created gaps — passes — in them so that people may travel from here to there. The mercy is doubled: the same ranges that steady the earth are cut through so they do not close anyone in.

And the ayah ends **لَعَلَّهُمْ يَهْتَدُونَ**, "that they may be guided" — the wording itself sets the traveller's road and guidance side by side.

## The sky: a roof, guarded (ayah 32)

**سَقْفًا مَحْفُوظًا** — a roof, safe and well-guarded. Ibn Kathir explains it as covering the earth like a dome above it, and gathers the parallel ayat: "With Hands We constructed the heaven. Verily, We are able to extend the vastness of space thereof" (51:47); "By the heaven and Him who built it" (91:5); "Have they not looked at the heaven above them, how We have made it and adorned it, and there are no rifts in it?" (50:6).

He adds a note on the building and making described in these ayat: it refers to the raising of the dome, as when the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said, **"Islam is built on five"** — meaning five pillars, which can only refer to a tent as familiar among the Arabs.

As for **مَحْفُوظًا**, Ibn Kathir says it means high, and protected from anything reaching it. Mujahid said simply: "Raised up."

## "Yet they turn away from its signs"

Here the passage lands its blow. After a roof, a stabilised earth, passes cut through mountains and life drawn out of water — *and they turn away from its signs*. Ibn Kathir compares it to "And how many a sign in the heavens and the earth they pass by, while they are averse therefrom" (12:105). They do not think, he says, about how Allah created the sky, so vast and high, and adorned it with heavenly bodies both stationary and moving by night and day — such as the sun, which completes its circuit in one day and night until it completes its allotted time, which no one knows except Allah, who created it, subjugated it and directed its course.

Read the charge carefully. It is not that the sign was missing or hidden. It is that they pass by it — the evidence is right over their heads — and are averse to it. That is not a shortage of information.

## The great clock (ayah 33)

Ibn Kathir reads ayah 33 as Allah drawing attention to some of His signs. **Night and day:** the one with its darkness and stillness, the other with its light and human interaction; sometimes the one is longer while the other is shorter, and then they switch. **The sun and the moon:** the sun with its own light and its own path and orbit and allotted time; the moon shining with a different light, travelling on a different path, with its own allotted time.

**كُلٌّ فِي فَلَكٍ يَسْبَحُونَ** — "each floating in an orbit." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains that **فَلَك (falak)** is used for a circle or anything round, which is why it is sometimes used for the sky itself; here it means the orbits of the sun and the moon in which they revolve. Ibn Kathir glosses *yasbaḥūn* as revolving, and quotes Ibn ʿAbbas: "They revolve like a spinning wheel, in a circle." He closes with 6:96 — "He is the Cleaver of the daybreak. He has appointed the night for resting, and the sun and the moon for reckoning. Such is the measuring of the All-Mighty, the All-Knowing" — which names the point exactly: this is *taqdīr*, precise measuring by One who is All-Mighty and All-Knowing.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds two observations: the Qurʼanic words do not specify the location of the orbits in space, and the ayah apparently indicates that the sun too moves around an orbit — something scientists previously did not believe, though the most modern research has now accepted it. Read alongside Muhammad Taqi Usmani's caution above, the lesson is the same: notice the confirmation, but let the Qurʼan stand on its own authority.

## Living it

**Recover the verb.** *Have they not seen* covers both what the eye observes and what the mind concludes. Rain that falls on dead ground, a mountain range, a sunrise — these are exhibits in an argument, not scenery. Let one of them, today, actually finish its sentence in your heart: *there is a Creator, and He alone deserves worship.*

**Fear the turning away more than the not-knowing.** Ayah 32 does not condemn people for lacking data. It condemns them for passing signs and being averse to them. Familiarity is the anaesthetic; the sky becomes wallpaper.

**Take the four deeds.** When Abu Hurayrah asked what would take him to Paradise, he was given: spread salām, feed people, keep the ties of kinship, and pray at night while others sleep. A person who has just understood that the origin of every living thing is water, and that the sky above him is a roof safe and well-guarded, has every reason to be the kind of person who greets strangers, feeds neighbours, calls his relatives, and stands before his Lord when nobody is watching.

passages.title: Every soul will taste death
passages.tafsir:
Two ayat that answer a taunt with a truth no one can argue with. The Makkans were waiting for the Prophet ﷺ to die; Allah replies that no human being was ever given permanent residence in this world — and then widens the answer far beyond the quarrel, until it takes in every soul who has ever lived, the death each one must taste, the good and bad days that test them on the way there, and the return to Allah at the end. Ayah 34 settles the argument; ayah 35 turns the argument into a mirror for the reader.

## The taunt behind ayah 34

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān — the Qur'an commentary this passage draws on alongside Ibn Kathīr — places these verses in the flow of what comes before them. The preceding ayat had given a strong and logical rebuttal of the exaggerated beliefs of the disbelievers and polytheists — the claim that Sayyidnā Masīḥ and Sayyidnā ʿUzayr (peace be upon them) were associates of Allah, or that the Messiah and the angels were Allah's children. Unable to come up with a satisfactory answer to the rational arguments the Qur'an put to them, the disbelievers of Makkah were left in despair, and fell back on the one hope left to a person who has lost the argument: they began to wish for the death of the Holy Prophet ﷺ.

Maʿārif notes that the Qur'an mentions this wish elsewhere too — in 52:30, نَّتَرَبَّصُ بِهِ رَيْبَ الْمَنُونِ, where they are quoted as sitting and waiting for death to take him. Their plan was not to refute him. It was to outlast him.

## Two answers packed into one verse

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws out two replies Allah Taʿālā gives to this pitiable wish.

**First**, even if the Holy Prophet ﷺ had died early, how would that have helped them? If they imagined they could use his death as an argument against his prophethood, they were badly mistaken — because all the other Prophets (peace be upon them), whose prophethood they themselves accepted, also died when their time came. If the death of their own prophets did not alter those men's position as prophets, how could the death of Muhammad ﷺ change his? That is the force of وَمَا جَعَلْنَا لِبَشَرٍ مِّن قَبْلِكَ الْخُلْدَ — *We did not assign immortality to any human even before you*. Death is not a verdict on a messenger's truthfulness. It is the standing arrangement for human beings.

**Second**, if their real purpose in wishing for his early death was simply to appease their own frustration, they should have known that death is universal, and everybody has to die sooner or later — including them. Maʿārif quotes a Persian couplet that puts the point with a dry smile:

> If an enemy dies, it is not to be rejoiced, because our own life is not eternal.

There is no revenge in outliving someone when you are standing in the same queue.

## The word that turns back on them

Notice the two words Allah sets facing each other in ayah 34. He denies **al-khuld** — permanent, unending abiding — to any human being before the Prophet ﷺ. Then He asks: *would they, then, be* **al-khālidūn** — the ones who abide forever? It is the same root thrown back at them. The very thing that has never been granted to a single human being is the thing they are quietly assuming for themselves while they wait for his funeral.

Ibn Kathīr is careful to fix the sense of الْخُلْد precisely: it means immortality **in this world**. He does not leave it as an abstract statement but anchors it in another ayah:

> *Whatsoever is on it (the earth) will perish. And the Face of your Lord full of majesty and honour will remain forever.* (55:26–27)

That pairing is the heart of the matter. Permanence is not something creation possesses in small quantities; it is what remains when everything on this earth has gone. Everything else is on its way out. Ibn Kathīr's comment on فَهُمُ الْخَالِدُونَ is blunt: they hope that they will live forever after you, but that will not happen — everything will pass away.

## "Every soul will taste death"

So Allah says, in ayah 35, كُلُّ نَفْسٍ ذَائِقَةُ الْمَوْتِ — *Every soul is going to taste death.* The argument with Quraysh has just become a statement about you.

**Who is included in "every soul"?** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that here the word *nafs* (soul) refers to the living things of the earth, all of whom must face death, and does not include the angels. As for whether the angels too will die on the Day of Judgement, Maʿārif reports a genuine difference of opinion among scholars, citing Rūḥ ul-Maʿānī — an earlier tafsir that Maʿārif quotes from for this material: some say that every living thing will die, if only momentarily, whether it belongs to the earth or to the skies; others maintain that the angels, and the ḥūr and ghilmān of Paradise, are excluded from this general rule. Maʿārif does not force the question shut, and neither should we — it closes with *only Allah knows best*.

**What is death?** On this, Maʿārif reports what the majority of scholars believe: death is the departure of the soul from the mortal human frame. The soul itself is a subtle, ethereal living thing, made of light, which resides in the human body — and Maʿārif gives a beautiful image for the manner of that residence: *just as fragrance resides in the rose*. It is not a part you could point to or cut out; it is present throughout, and when it leaves, what is left is no longer the same thing. Maʿārif adds that Ibn al-Qayyim proved this point convincingly in his book (as cited in Rūḥ ul-Maʿānī).

**Why "taste"?** The Qur'an did not say every soul will *meet* death or *undergo* it. It says every soul is a **taster** of death — ذَائِقَة. Maʿārif draws the implication out: the term means that every individual will feel the pain of death, because considering the manner in which body and soul are joined together, their separation should obviously entail some pain. Tasting is first-hand. Nobody experiences it by report; nobody is anaesthetised through it. It is knowledge you acquire only by going through it yourself.

**Does that leave no room for the friends of Allah?** Maʿārif anticipates the objection. There are saintly persons who regard death as a deliverance from the trials and tribulations of worldly life and as a means of bringing them closer to their Supreme love, that is Allah. But, Maʿārif is clear, this pleasure does not negate the agony of death — *because where the reward is high, a little pain is easily tolerated*. The two are not rivals. A person can dread the wrench and still long for the meeting, in the same breath.

## "And We shall test you with evil and with good"

The second half of ayah 35 explains what the interval before that tasting is for: وَنَبْلُوكُم بِالشَّرِّ وَالْخَيْرِ فِتْنَةً — *We test you with evil and with good by way of trial.*

Ibn Kathīr paraphrases: "We shall test you, sometimes with difficulties and sometimes with ease, to see who will give thanks and who will be ungrateful, who will have patience and who will despair." Two pairs, and they do not line up the way we assume. We tend to imagine hardship tests patience and that is the end of it. Here, ease is a test in its own right, with its own way of failing.

Ibn Kathīr then reports from Ibn ʿAbbās, through the narration of ʿAlī bin Abī Ṭalḥah, a striking expansion of what "evil and good" covers:

> with difficulties and with times of prosperity, with health and sickness, with richness and poverty, with lawful and unlawful, obedience and sin, with guidance and misguidance.

Read that list slowly. It begins where we expect — circumstances that happen *to* a person — and then keeps going into things a person moves through and chooses within. Lawful and unlawful are a test. Obedience and sin are a test. Guidance and misguidance are a test. On this reading from Ibn ʿAbbās, there is no neutral ground in a human life, no stretch of it that is merely happening. Every condition you find yourself in is a question being put to you.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān lays out the same two-sided test in plain terms: **sharr** (bad) includes unpleasant things such as illness, grief, pain and poverty; **khayr** (good) means desirable things — good health, happiness, comfort and abundance. Man is subjected to these conditions in this world for a test, and the test is that he should show patience and endurance in the face of adversity, and offer thanks to Allah when his life is peaceful and comfortable.

Note also the word فِتْنَةً, given at the end: the whole arrangement is *a trial*. Not an accident, not a random distribution of luck. Whatever has landed on you was assigned, and it was assigned in order to reveal something.

**The harder half.** Maʿārif reports that wise men have said something most of us have backwards: it is more difficult to be steadfast and consistent in offering thanks to Allah for His gifts than to persevere and show patience in difficult circumstances. And it cites the words of Sayyidnā ʿUmar (may Allah be pleased with him), as reported in Rūḥ ul-Maʿānī:

> "We were tested by discomforts and we bore it with patience, but when we were tested by pleasures, we could not observe patience" — that is, we could not offer gratitude to Allah as was due.

That is one of the great men of this ummah saying that his generation passed the hard exam and struggled with the easy one. Hardship pushes a person towards Allah almost by reflex; comfort quietly persuades him he no longer needs to lean on anyone. The list of losses in a person's life is easy to recite. The list of mercies is so long we stop counting — and stop noticing.

## "And to Us you will be returned"

The passage closes the loop: وَإِلَيْنَا تُرْجَعُونَ. Ibn Kathīr's comment is short and final — *and We will requite you according to your deeds*. Death is not the point of the passage; it is the doorway in it. The test has an examiner, the examiner has a record, and the record has a settling. Everything the Makkans were waiting for — the funeral, the silence, the field left to themselves — turns out to be the beginning of the part they had not thought about at all.

## Living it

The passage asks for something very concrete.

**Stop measuring your life against other people's.** Quraysh's whole strategy was to outlast a man. It was worthless as a strategy because their own permanence was never on the table. Any plan whose payoff depends on being here later is built on ground ayah 34 has already removed.

**Expect the good days to test you too.** If you only brace for hardship, you will be ambushed by ease. Maʿārif's guidance is a simple two-part discipline: *ṣabr* (patience) in adversity, *shukr* (gratitude) in comfort — and ʿUmar's confession is a warning that the second is where able people slip.

**Read your present circumstances as a question.** The list reported from Ibn ʿAbbās means that your health, your wealth, what is in front of you that is lawful and what is unlawful, are all part of the same examination. There is no off-duty portion of a life.

**Let the certainty of tasting death do its work now.** Every soul will taste it; you will feel it; and immediately beyond it is the return and the requital. That is not a thought meant to freeze a believer. It is meant to make him spend his good days gratefully and his hard days patiently, because he knows what the days are for.

passages.title: Mockers who hasten the promised Hour
passages.tafsir:
These six ayat hold one scene and Allah's answer to it: the disbelievers of Quraysh sneering at the Prophet ﷺ as he passes, and demanding that the promised punishment be produced on the spot. Ibn Kathir's own headings for this stretch name the movement exactly — "How the Idolators mocked the Prophet (ﷺ)", then "The Idolators seek to hasten on the Punishment", then "The Lessons to be learned from Those Who mocked the Messengers in the Past". What runs through all of it is **haste**: their impatience to see the threat arrive, the believers' impatience to see the mockers answered, and against both, Allah's own timing — which delays, and then does not delay for an instant.

## The sneer, and what it exposed

Ibn Kathir identifies the people in ayah 36 precisely: "the disbelievers of the Quraysh, such as Abu Jahl and his like." This is not faceless opposition. These were named men who knew the Prophet ﷺ personally and turned him into a joke when they saw him.

**إِن يَتَّخِذُونَكَ إِلَّا هُزُوًا** — "they take you not except for mockery." The rendering itself says it: mockery was the whole of their response. Ibn Kathir glosses it as making fun of him and insulting him.

Their line was: **أَهَٰذَا الَّذِي يَذْكُرُ آلِهَتَكُمْ** — "Is this the one who talks about your gods?" Ibn Kathir unpacks the tone behind it: *is this the one who insults your gods and ridicules your intelligence?* That second half is worth noticing. The grievance was not only that their idols were being criticised; they heard in his message the charge that they were fools for worshipping them.

And Allah answers in the same breath: **وَهُم بِذِكْرِ الرَّحْمَٰنِ هُمْ كَافِرُونَ** — "While they disbelieve at the mention of the Most Gracious." Ibn Kathir states it plainly: "they disbelieve in Allah and yet they mock the Messenger of Allah ﷺ." Men outraged on behalf of their gods, and unmoved — worse, disbelieving — at the mention of the Most Gracious.

Ibn Kathir sets a parallel beside it, where the same kind of crowd says: "Is this the one whom Allah has sent as a Messenger? He would have nearly misled us from our gods, had it not been that we were patient and constant in their worship!" — and the scene closes: "And they will know, when they see the torment, who it is that is most astray from the path!" (25:41–42). The mockery is on record. So is the verdict — deferred, not cancelled.

## Why "man is created of haste" comes here

Then a line that looks, at first, like a change of subject: **خُلِقَ الْإِنسَانُ مِنْ عَجَلٍ** — "Man is created of haste."

Ibn Kathir explains the placement directly: "The reason why the haste of man is mentioned here is that when mention is made of those who mock the Messenger ﷺ, (the believers) will want to avenge them swiftly, and that so should happen sooner."

So the ayah turns, mid-scene, from the mockers to the ones hearing about the mockers. The believing heart wants the matter settled now. Allah names that reflex — and then describes His own way instead: He delays the punishment, says Ibn Kathir, "until a time when, once He seizes him, He will never let him go. He delays it, then He hastens it; He waits, then He does not delay any longer."

The same impatience runs on both sides of the scene. Ibn Kathir notes that the idolaters, for their part, "seek to hasten punishment upon themselves, out of denial, rejection, disbelief, stubbornness and a belief that it will never happen." Their "When will this promise come to pass, if you are truthful?" (ayah 38) is not a request for information; it is spoken by men who are certain nothing is coming.

## What ʿajal means — and what it does not

Maarif ul Quran opens the word up. **عَجَل** ('ajal) means haste or hurry, and it is used "in situations when one desires things to happen before their time, and this trait is bad by its very nature." That is the defect being named: not speed as such, but wanting the fruit before the season. The same weakness is named elsewhere — **وَكَانَ الْإِنسَانُ عَجُولًا**, "Man is prone to haste" (17:11), "meaning that he is very impatient." Maarif ul Quran adds that when Sayyidna Musa (peace be upon him) went to Mount Tur in a hurry, leaving his people behind, he was censured by Allah.

Then comes the distinction that keeps the ayah from being misread as a rebuke of religious eagerness. Maarif ul Quran points out that the Prophets (peace be upon them) and the devout who try to excel one another in righteous deeds "have been commended and their zeal to do good deeds does not constitute haste and hurry because they do not try to do these deeds before their time. In fact they do the deeds on time, but try to excel each other in quantity and quality."

Racing to do a good deed at its appointed moment is virtue. Demanding an outcome before its appointed moment is ʿajal.

And why "created *of* haste"? Maarif ul Quran explains it as an Arab usage: when a man is identified by some intrinsic trait of his character, the Arabs would say he is "made of" that trait — "a short tempered man would be called a 'man made of anger'." So the ayah means that haste "is one of the many weaknesses which are inherent in human nature," not that man is literally composed of it. Recognising the reflex as native to you is itself the beginning of not obeying it.

## "I will show you My signs"

**سَأُرِيكُمْ آيَاتِي فَلَا تَسْتَعْجِلُونِ** — "I will show you My Ayat. So ask Me not to hasten (them)."

Two readings are offered in the sources, and both belong here.

Ibn Kathir takes **آيَاتِي** to mean "My vengeance, ruling and power over those who disobey Me." On that reading the signs are the reckoning itself, and the warning is that they are demanding something they would not want delivered.

Maarif ul Quran, citing Qurtubi, takes the signs to be "those miracles and events which bear evidence to the honesty of the Holy Prophet ﷺ and the truth of his message" — and adds that these "also occurred during the battle of Badr, when the Muslims who were considered weak and worthy of contempt gained a great victory over their enemies."

Either way, the answer to "hurry it up" is: it is coming, on a schedule that is not yours.

## The answer they were given instead of a date

Allah never gives them the "when." He addresses the confidence behind the question instead.

**لَوْ يَعْلَمُ الَّذِينَ كَفَرُوا** — "If only those who disbelieved knew…" Ibn Kathir fills in what such knowledge would produce: "if only they knew for certain that it will inevitably come to pass, they would not seek to hasten it."

Then the picture: **حِينَ لَا يَكُفُّونَ عَن وُجُوهِهِمُ النَّارَ وَلَا عَن ظُهُورِهِمْ** — the time when they will not be able to ward off the Fire from their faces, nor from their backs. Ibn Kathir gathers the ayat that fill this out — "They shall have coverings of Fire, above them and coverings beneath them" (39:16); "Theirs will be a bed of Hell, and over them coverings of Hellfire" (7:41); "Their garments will be of tar, and fire will cover their faces" (14:50) — and sums it up: "The torment will surround them on all sides."

**وَلَا هُمْ يُنصَرُونَ** — "and they will not be helped." Ibn Kathir: "they will have no helper," as in "And they have no guardian against Allah" (13:34).

Ayah 40 then answers the "when" in the only way it is ever answered — by naming not a date but a *manner*. Ibn Kathir takes it clause by clause:

- **بَلْ تَأْتِيهِم بَغْتَةً** — "Nay, it will come upon them all of a sudden": it "will come upon them suddenly, i.e., it will take them by surprise."
- **فَتَبْهَتُهُمْ** — "and will perplex them": "it will scare them, and they will succumb to it in confusion, not knowing what they are doing."
- **فَلَا يَسْتَطِيعُونَ رَدَّهَا** — "and they will have no power to avert it": "they will have no means of doing so."
- **وَلَا هُمْ يُنظَرُونَ** — "nor will they get respite": "it will not be delayed for them even for an instant."

Read the four together and the trap closes: no warning, no composure, no defence, no extra time. The men demanding a timetable are told that the one thing they will never be given is notice.

## Consolation, and the pattern he ﷺ stands inside

The passage ends by lifting the Prophet's ﷺ eyes off his own street. **وَلَقَدِ اسْتُهْزِئَ بِرُسُلٍ مِّن قَبْلِكَ** — "Indeed, Messengers were mocked before you."

Ibn Kathir reads the ayah as Allah "consoling His Messenger ﷺ for the pain and insult caused by the mockery and disbelief of the idolators." That word — pain — is Ibn Kathir's own. The Qur'an does not pretend the ridicule did not hurt him ﷺ. It steadies him by showing him the pattern he stands inside.

Then the close: **فَحَاقَ بِالَّذِينَ سَخِرُوا مِنْهُم مَّا كَانُوا بِهِ يَسْتَهْزِئُونَ** — "but the scoffers were surrounded by what they used to mock." Ibn Kathir identifies what that was: "the punishment which they thought would never come to pass." The very thing they treated as an empty threat became the thing that closed around them.

And beside it he sets: "Verily, Messengers were denied before you, but with patience they bore the denial, and they were hurt; till Our help reached them, and none can alter the Words of Allah" (6:34). Note the order in that verse: denial, patience, hurt — and *then* the help. The help is certain. The sequence is not negotiable.

## Living it

**This passage is training for anyone whose faith is treated as a joke.**

- **Expect it; do not read it as failure.** Ayah 41 states plainly that Messengers were mocked before him ﷺ. Ridicule is not evidence that something has gone wrong.
- **Your urge to see them answered *now* is the very trait ayah 37 names.** Ibn Kathir ties the mention of human haste directly to the believers' wish to avenge the Messenger ﷺ swiftly. Knowing the reflex is built in is what lets you decline to act on it.
- **Distinguish the two speeds.** Following Maarif ul Quran: competing in good deeds — doing them on time, and excelling in quantity and quality — is commended. Wanting things "to happen before their time" is the weakness being corrected.
- **Do not confuse delay with absence.** Ibn Kathir's formulation answers the mocker's assumption and the believer's impatience at once: "He delays it, then He hastens it; He waits, then He does not delay any longer."
- **Leave the timing where it belongs.** They asked "when?" and were never told. Neither are we. What we are told is the manner — sudden, stunning, unavertable, without an instant's respite — and that is enough to live differently today.

passages.title: No protector, and the just scales
passages.tafsir:
These six ayat answer the mockery the Prophet ﷺ was enduring from the idolaters with a single question they cannot answer: *who is keeping you alive?* From there the passage moves outward — to false gods who cannot protect even themselves, to the comfortable lifespans that lulled the deniers into thinking they were safe, and finally to the Balance of the Day of Resurrection, where every deed down to a mustard seed is brought forward. The thread holding it together is **protection and accounting**: no one shields you from Allah in this world, and no one shields you from the reckoning in the next.

## The setting: consoling a mocked Messenger

Ibn Kathir notes that in the preceding ayah (41) Allah is **consoling His Messenger ﷺ for the pain and insult caused by the mockery and disbelief of the idolaters**. Messengers before him were mocked too — and then "the scoffers were surrounded by what they used to mock." Ibn Kathir explains that phrase as *the punishment which they thought would never come to pass*. The joke closed in on the ones telling it.

He draws the parallel to Sūrat al-Anʿām: "Verily, Messengers were denied before you, but with patience they bore the denial, and they were hurt; till Our help reached them, and none can alter the Words of Allah" (6:34). The shape of the passage is set before ayah 42 begins: *you are not the first, and the words of Allah cannot be altered.*

## Ayah 42 — "Who guards you, night and day?"

Ibn Kathir says Allah now **mentions His favour to His creatures**: He protects them by night and by day, taking care of them and watching over them "with His Eye that never sleeps." That is what the ayah trades on: the reason you woke up this morning is not luck.

**The verb يَكْلَؤُكُم (yaklaʾukum)** is rendered by Ibn Kathir as *"guard and protect."* It is the language of a watchman standing over someone who cannot defend himself. And the ayah names **بِٱلَّيْلِ وَٱلنَّهَارِ**, "by night and by day," so no hour is left out.

Then comes the turn that makes the ayah bite: guarded **مِنَ ٱلرَّحْمَٰنِ — from the Most Gracious.** Ibn Kathir's gloss: *"other than the Most Gracious Himself?"* If Allah decided to seize you, who would step in? And note the name chosen: not "from the Overpowering" or "from the Avenger," but **from ar-Raḥmān.** The One you would need protecting from is the One whose mercy is the reason you are not being seized. There is no third party in the universe.

**بَلْ هُمْ عَن ذِكْرِ رَبِّهِم مُّعْرِضُونَ** — "Nay, but they turn away from the remembrance of their Lord." Ibn Kathir explains this as: *they do not recognise the blessings and favour of Allah towards them; they turn away from His signs and blessings.* The ayah does not accuse them of failing to *find* an answer; it accuses them of not being interested in the question. Turning away (iʿrāḍ) is not a failure of intellect but a decision of the heart.

## Ayah 43 — gods who cannot save themselves

**أَمْ لَهُمْ ءَالِهَةٌ تَمْنَعُهُم مِّن دُونِنَا** — "Or do they have gods, other than Us, who can protect them?"

Ibn Kathir identifies this as **a rhetorical question aimed at denouncing and rebuking** — it is not asking for information; it exposes an absurdity. The meaning, he says: *do they have any gods who can protect them and take care of them other than Us? It is not as they imagine or as they claim.*

Then the ayah answers itself twice over:

- **لَا يَسْتَطِيعُونَ نَصْرَ أَنفُسِهِمْ** — "They have no power to help themselves." Ibn Kathir: *these gods on whom they rely instead of Allah cannot even help themselves.* The bar is humiliatingly low — not "can they help you," but "can they help *themselves*" — and they fail even that.
- **وَلَا هُم مِّنَّا يُصْحَبُونَ** — "nor can they be protected from Us." Ibn Kathir cites **al-ʿAwfī reporting from Ibn ʿAbbās**: *"Nor can they be guarded from Us."* The false objects of worship are not merely powerless helpers; they need a guardian as badly as their worshippers do.

Read ayat 42 and 43 together: there is exactly one Guardian, He is *ar-Raḥmān*, and every alternative you might reach for is itself unguarded.

## Ayah 44 — the deception of a long, comfortable life

**بَلْ مَتَّعْنَا هَٰٓؤُلَآءِ وَءَابَآءَهُمْ حَتَّىٰ طَالَ عَلَيْهِمُ ٱلْعُمُرُ** — "Nay, We gave the luxuries of this life to these men and their fathers until the period grew long for them."

Ibn Kathir names the psychology: they have been **deceived and misled by the luxuries that they enjoy in this world and the long life that they have been given, so they believe that they are following something good.** They had no argument for their idolatry — ayah 43 has just destroyed it. What they had instead was *duration*: our fathers lived this way, we have lived this way, nothing bad has happened, therefore we must be right. Prosperity was mistaken for proof.

Then Allah warns them: **أَفَلَا يَرَوْنَ أَنَّا نَأْتِى ٱلْأَرْضَ نَنقُصُهَا مِنْ أَطْرَافِهَا** — "See they not that We gradually reduce the land (in their control) from its outlying borders?"

Ibn Kathir sets this beside al-Aḥqāf: "And indeed We have destroyed towns round about you, and We have shown the Ayat in various ways that they might return" (46:27). And he records that **al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī said: "This means the victory of Islam over disbelief."**

Ibn Kathir joins both readings into one lesson: *do they not learn a lesson from the fact that Allah supported the believers against their enemies, destroyed the disbelieving nations and the evil-doing townships, and saved His believing servants?* The ground under their assumptions is being eaten away at the edges — ruined settlements behind them in history, the advance of Islam over disbelief — while they read their long comfortable lives as a guarantee.

**أَفَهُمُ ٱلْغَٰلِبُونَ** — "Is it then they who will overcome?" Ibn Kathir: *on the contrary, they are the ones who will be overcome, who will be defeated, humiliated and brought low.*

## Ayah 45 — "I warn you only by revelation"

**قُلْ إِنَّمَآ أُنذِرُكُم بِٱلْوَحْىِ.** Ibn Kathir puts the words in the Prophet's ﷺ mouth: *'I only convey to you the warning of Allah's punishment and vengeance, and this is no more than that which Allah reveals to me.'*

The restriction particle **إِنَّمَا ("only")** does two jobs. It defends the Prophet ﷺ — he is not inventing threats or settling scores; he transmits. And it raises the stakes: if the warning is revelation, arguing with the messenger is pointless, because the message is not his.

**وَلَا يَسْمَعُ ٱلصُّمُّ ٱلدُّعَآءَ إِذَا مَا يُنذَرُونَ** — "But the deaf will not hear the call, even when they are warned." Ibn Kathir comments that the warning **is of no benefit to the one whom Allah has made blind and has put a seal over his hearing and his heart.** The deafness is not a physical defect but a settled condition of the soul: the sound arrives, the meaning does not. This connects back to ayah 42 — *they turn away from the remembrance of their Lord*. Persistent turning away hardens into inability to hear.

## Ayah 46 — a single breath of it

**وَلَئِن مَّسَّتْهُمْ نَفْحَةٌ مِّنْ عَذَابِ رَبِّكَ لَيَقُولُنَّ يَٰوَيْلَنَآ إِنَّا كُنَّا ظَٰلِمِينَ** — "And if a breath of the torment of your Lord touches them, they will surely cry: 'Woe unto us! Indeed we have been wrongdoers!'"

Every word here is chosen to be as small as possible. Not the punishment, but **نَفْحَة (nafḥa)** — a *breath* of it. Not "descends upon them" but **مَسَّتْهُمْ**, merely *touches* them. And even that is only a breath **min** — from, i.e. a portion of — the torment of your Lord. Ibn Kathir's summary is exact: *if these disbelievers were affected by the slightest touch of Allah's punishment, they would confess their sins and admit that they had wronged themselves in this world.*

Set that against the confidence of men secure enough to mock a Prophet ﷺ: they would collapse into "**yā waylanā**, woe to us!" at a breath of what they were warned about. Note what they confess — not "the warning was true" but **إِنَّا كُنَّا ظَٰلِمِينَ**, "we ourselves were the wrongdoers." Under the smallest pressure the truth comes out whole.

## Ayah 47 — the scales of justice

**وَنَضَعُ ٱلْمَوَٰزِينَ ٱلْقِسْطَ لِيَوْمِ ٱلْقِيَٰمَةِ فَلَا تُظْلَمُ نَفْسٌ شَيْـًٔا** — "And We shall set up the Balances of justice for the Day of Resurrection, so that no soul will be dealt with unjustly in anything."

**One balance or many?** Maʿārif ul Qurʾān explains that **مَوَازِين (mawāzīn)** is the plural of **مِيزَان (mīzān)**, which means a scale, and that the plural has been understood in two ways. Some exegetes held that many scales will be used — different balances for different individuals, or different balances for different types of deeds. But **the majority of scholars agree that there will be only one balance** to weigh all the deeds, the plural being used because that one Balance will serve the purpose of many balances: it measures the deeds of all the children of Ādam (ʿalayhi as-salām) from the earliest time to the Day of Judgment, whose count only Allah knows. Ibn Kathir reports the same position — *the majority of scholars state that it is one Balance, and the plural form is used here to reflect the large number of deeds which will be weighed therein.*

**ٱلْقِسْط (al-qisṭ)**, Maʿārif notes, means *justice and fairness*. So the meaning of the ayah, he says, is that the Balance will measure fairly and justly and no injustice will be done to anyone — which is exactly the consequence the ayah then states: **not one soul is wronged in anything.**

Maʿārif also transmits several reports about that Day, naming its sources:

- **Mustadrak of Ḥākim**, through Sayyidunā Salmān (raḍiya Allāhu ʿanhu), that the Prophet ﷺ said the balance used on the Day of Judgment for weighing deeds will be so enormous in size and span that it could enclose the earth and the sky within its fold. (Maẓharī)
- **Ḥāfiẓ Abū al-Qāsim Lālkāʾī**, in his *Sunan*, through Sayyidunā Anas (raḍiya Allāhu ʿanhu), that the Prophet ﷺ said an angel will be posted on the balance and every man brought before it: if his good deeds outweigh his sins the angel will announce loudly, so that everyone present hears, that so-and-so has passed his test and will never be deprived of anything again; and if his sins outweigh his virtues, the angel will announce that the wretched so-and-so has failed and been made destitute forever. Lālkāʾī also reports, on the authority of Sayyidunā Ḥudhayfah (raḍiya Allāhu ʿanhu), that the angel posted on the balance is none other than Jibrīl (ʿalayhi as-salām).
- **Ḥākim, Bayhaqī and ʿĀjurrī**, through Sayyidah ʿĀʾishah (raḍiya Allāhu ʿanhā), that she asked the Prophet ﷺ whether he would remember his family members on the Day of Judgment. He replied that on that Day there will be three occasions when no one will remember anyone: first, when people are brought before the scale of justice for the weighing of their deeds, until it is known whether one's virtues outweigh his sins; second, when the records of deeds are thrown in the air, until they are placed in the right hand — a sign of salvation — or in the left hand or from behind; and third, the crossing of the bridge of Ṣirāṭ, until that bridge is crossed.

**How are deeds weighed?** Maʿārif gives two possibilities. One: the deeds recorded by the angels are themselves weighed — as indicated by the well-known *ḥadīth al-biṭāqah*, the hadith of the card, in which a card bearing *lā ilāha illā Allāh* is placed in the balance and outweighs a heap of bad deeds (so noted by Muhammad Taqi Usmani). Two: the deeds are converted into substances which are then weighed. Maʿārif states that **by and large the traditions support the second view, and a majority of scholars have adopted it**, confirmed by ayat such as "And they will find what they did all there" (18:49). This is a genuine difference among the scholars; both are reported, and neither should be presented as the only view.

**Not a mustard seed escapes.** **وَإِن كَانَ مِثْقَالَ حَبَّةٍ مِّنْ خَرْدَلٍ أَتَيْنَا بِهَا** — "And if there be the weight of a mustard seed, We will bring it." Maʿārif: on the Day of Reckoning *all the deeds of every person, big or small, good or bad, will be brought forth* so that they may be subjected to reckoning and weighing. Ibn Kathir gathers the parallel ayat: "and your Lord treats no one with injustice" (18:49); "Surely, Allah wrongs not even the weight of a speck of dust, but if there is any good, He doubles it, and gives from Him a great reward" (4:40); and Luqmān's advice to his son, that a mustard-seed's weight "though it be in a rock, or in the heavens or in the earth, Allah will bring it forth" (31:16).

Together they show the asymmetry mercy introduces: nothing is too small to be counted, and the smallest *good* is not merely counted but doubled. Then: **وَكَفَىٰ بِنَا حَٰسِبِينَ** — "And sufficient are We to take account."

## From the Sunnah

**In the Two Ṣaḥīḥs**, from Abū Hurayrah (raḍiya Allāhu ʿanhu), that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: *"Two words which are light on the tongue, heavy in the Balance and beloved to ar-Raḥmān: Subḥān Allāhi wa bi-ḥamdih, Subḥān Allāhi'l-ʿAẓīm."* Weight in the Balance and effort in this world are not the same currency — and the hadith names Him **ar-Raḥmān**, the same name as in ayah 42.

**Imam Aḥmad recorded** — and Maʿārif ul Qurʾān cites the same incident from **Tirmidhī** (via Qurṭubī) — from ʿĀʾishah (raḍiya Allāhu ʿanhā), that one of the Companions of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ sat down before him and said: "O Messenger of Allah, I have two slaves who lie to me, betray me and disobey me, and I hit them and insult them. How do I stand with regard to them?" The Prophet ﷺ answered that the extent to which they betrayed, disobeyed and lied to him will be measured against the punishment he meted out: if his punishment was commensurate with their misconduct, he will be equal and nothing will be counted for him or against him; if it was *less* than they deserved, this will count in his favour; and if it was *more* than they deserved, then Allah will take what is due to them from him.

The man began to weep. The Prophet ﷺ asked, *"What is the matter with him? Has he not read the words of Allah — 'And We shall set up Balances of justice on the Day of Resurrection…'?"* The man said: "O Messenger of Allah, I think there is nothing better than keeping away from these people" — meaning his slaves — "I call upon you to bear witness that they are all free."

That is the ayah working on a living heart. He did not hear a doctrine about the afterlife; he heard an audit of his own household.

## Living it

**Wake up to the Guard.** Ayah 42 asks a question you are meant to keep answering. Ibn Kathir's charge against the deniers was not that they reasoned badly but that they *did not recognise the blessings and favour of Allah towards them.* The cure is dhikr — the very thing they turned away from.

**Do not read comfort as approval.** Ayah 44 warns against the inference we all make: things are going well, therefore I must be fine. Ibn Kathir says plainly that long life and easy circumstances had deceived them into believing they were following something good. A long life is a gift, not a verdict.

**Take small things seriously in both directions.** A mustard seed is brought forward. So the two light words are worth saying — and the small injustice, a little more punishment than was deserved, is worth undoing now, while undoing is still cheap. The report Ibn Kathir and Maʿārif both preserve concerns anyone whose position makes it safe for you to be unfair to them. On that Day, the safety runs the other way.

passages.title: The Criterion given, the Reminder revealed
passages.tafsir:
These three ayat place two revelations side by side — the Book given to Musa and Harun (peace be upon them), and the Qur'an being recited to those who rejected it — and then turn the comparison into a question aimed straight at the listener. Ayah 48 describes what Allah gave the earlier prophets; ayah 49 describes the kind of person that gift benefits; ayah 50 says *this* Book is a blessed Reminder sent down by Allah — "will you then deny it?"

## Allah pairs Musa with Muhammad ﷺ, and their Books with each other

Ibn Kathir opens his comment on this passage with an observation that unlocks it: "Allah often mentions Musa and Muhammad together — may the peace and blessings of Allah be upon them both — and He often mentions their Books together as well." He titles the whole section "The Revelation of the Tawrah and the Qur'an."

That is the architecture of these three ayat. Ayah 48 is not a detour into ancient history; it is laying a foundation. Allah gave a criterion, a light and a reminder before — and ayah 50 announces that He has sent down another. Only then does the question come: *will you then deny it?*

Notice too that the gift in ayah 48 is given to **Musa *and* Harun** together — both brothers named as recipients of the one grant.

## The three things they were given

**al-Furqān — the Criterion.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān defines it as that "which differentiates between right and wrong." The early commentators quoted by Ibn Kathir take it as the revealed Scripture itself, precisely because that is what a Scripture does:

- **Mujahid** said it means "the Scripture."
- **Abu Salih** said: "The Tawrah."
- **Qatadah** said: "The Tawrah, what it permits and it forbids, and how Allah differentiated between truth and falsehood."

Qatadah's answer is the fullest: the Tawrah is a *furqān* because it draws lines. It says *this* is lawful and *that* is not; *this* is true and *that* is false. Ibn Kathir then draws the conclusion for all revelation: "the heavenly Books included the distinction between truth and falsehood, guidance and misguidance, transgression and the right way, lawful and unlawful, and that which will fill the heart with light, guidance, fear of Allah and repentance."

Read that list slowly. Four pairs of opposites — and then something that is not a distinction at all but an effect: the Book *fills the heart* with light, guidance, fear of Allah and turning back to Him. A criterion in the hands of a living heart does not stay a chart of categories. It becomes light.

**Ḍiyā' — a shining light.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains this as what "provides light and manifestation of truth to hearts." The distinction is worth pausing on: the Criterion tells you *where the line is*; the Light lets you *see* it. Revelation gives both the map and the eyes.

**Dhikr — a Reminder, an advice.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān calls it "a source of guidance for the people," and Ibn Kathir glosses "a Reminder for those who have Taqwa" as "a reminder and exhortation for them." Revelation does not only inform; it exhorts — it presses on the listener.

So: a standard to judge by, a light to see by, and a voice of reminder and exhortation. Then comes the striking part.

## Why "for those who have Taqwa"?

The three gifts are described as being **li'l-muttaqīn** — for those who have taqwa, those mindful of Allah. But a revealed Book is not sent only to the pious few. Why name them?

The passage itself supplies the answer: it does not leave the word abstract. As Ibn Kathir puts it, "Then He describes them as" — and ayah 49 follows immediately with a portrait.

## The portrait in ayah 49

**"Those who fear their Lord in the unseen (bi'l-ghayb), and they are afraid of the Hour."**

Two clauses, and between them they cover a believer's whole inner life — his relationship with Allah, and his relationship with what is coming.

The first is fear of the Lord *bi'l-ghayb*, "in the unseen" — the rendering offered with this ayah is "who are in awe of their Lord without seeing Him." They have not laid eyes on their Lord, and yet He is real to them. Ibn Kathir gathers two other ayat that use this same phrase, and they are worth having in view because of what they add:

> "Who feared the Most Gracious in the unseen and came with a repenting heart." (50:33)

> "Verily, those who fear their Lord unseen, theirs will be forgiveness and a great reward." (67:12)

Two things stand out in what those ayat themselves say. In 50:33, the One feared unseen is named **the Most Gracious**, and what the one who fears Him brings is *a repenting heart* — a heart that turns back toward Him. And in 67:12, this same hidden fear — the kind no one else can see — is exactly what is met with "forgiveness and a great reward." What is invisible to people is fully known to Allah.

The second clause: **wa hum mina's-sāʿati mushfiqūn** — "and they are afraid of the Hour." Ibn Kathir's gloss is deliberately plain: "means, they fear it." And note what joins the two clauses: it is the *unseen* they fear — a Lord they have not seen, and an Hour that has not yet come. That is precisely the kind of heart a *dhikr*, a Reminder, reaches.

## A second reading of *al-Furqān*

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reports that some explain *furqān* here not as the Book but as the help of Allah, which was available to Sayyidna Musa (peace be upon him) at all times. The commentary then traces where that help was manifest in his life:

- He was **raised in the Pharaoh's house**.
- Then at the time of his **contest with the Egyptian magicians**, which resulted in the Pharaoh's discomfiture.
- And again when he was **pursued by the Pharaoh and his army**: Allah saved him by causing dry passageways to appear in the river and, after the Bani Isra'il had crossed over to the other side, by drowning the Pharaoh and his army.

And, as the commentary adds, "Even after this incident Allah's help was available to him at all times."

**The grammar behind the second reading.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān treats all three words — criterion, light and advice — as attributes of the Torah, but then reports that **Qurtubi** pointed out that whereas *ḍiyā'* (light) and *dhikr* (advice) are attributes of the Torah, *furqān* (criterion) is something else and not an attribute of the Torah, because of the use of the conjunctive letter **wa** ("and") after the word *al-furqān*.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān closes the point exactly as a careful scholar should — "Allah knows best" — and that is how we should hold it too. The reading given by Mujahid, Abu Salih and Qatadah, and adopted by Ibn Kathir, is that *al-furqān* is the Scripture itself. The alternative, reported by Maʿārif ul Qurʼān with Qurtubi's grammatical note, is that it is Allah's help to Musa. Both are readings passed down by scholars of standing, and the honest thing is to hold them as they are held in the books: side by side, with *Allah knows best*.

## Ayah 50: "And this is a blessed Reminder"

Now the pivot. Everything said about the earlier revelation is claimed for this one.

**"A Reminder" — dhikr.** The same word used in ayah 48. The Qur'an is not a rival to what came before; it is named with the same word.

**"Blessed" — mubārak.** And **"which We have sent down" — anzalnāhu**: the verb is Allah's own, spoken in the first person. It came *down*, and the One who sent it says so Himself.

The ayah opens with "And **this**" — and Ibn Kathir tells us what "this" is. His comment on the whole clause, "And this is a blessed Reminder which We have sent down," is a portrait of the Book's dignity: "the Magnificent Qur'an, which falsehood cannot approach, from before it or behind it, revealed by the All-Wise, Worthy of all praise." Falsehood has no way in — not from ahead of it, not from behind it. And it comes from One whom Ibn Kathir names by two of His own descriptions: All-Wise, and Worthy of all praise.

**"Will you then deny it?" — afa-antum lahu munkirūn.** The passage ends not with a statement but with a question. Ibn Kathir renders its force: "will you deny it when it is the utmost in clarity and truth?"

Feel the sequence one more time, because that is where the weight lies. Allah gave a criterion, a light and a reminder before. He has now sent down another, blessed, from the All-Wise, with no way in for falsehood. It is, in Ibn Kathir's words, the utmost in clarity and truth. *And you are the ones denying it?*

## Living it

**Have you let the Book become a criterion?** Ayah 48 says that is what Scripture is *for* — it differentiates between right and wrong. The practical test is simple: when your opinion and the Book differ, which one moves?

**Cultivate the fear that no one sees.** Ayah 49 makes fear of the Lord *in the unseen* the mark of the person described here, and the ayah Ibn Kathir cites alongside it (67:12) attaches "forgiveness and a great reward" to that same hidden fear. This is the part of religion with no audience — what you do when alone, what you refuse when no one would know.

**Keep the Hour in view.** "And they are afraid of the Hour" — Ibn Kathir says simply, "they fear it." Not a morbid dread, but the seriousness of someone who has not forgotten where this life is heading.

**Do not read ayah 50 as though it were about other people.** The question "will you then deny it?" is put to those who rejected outright — but a Book affirmed with the tongue and left unread has not really been received as *dhikr mubārak* either. The gift described in ayah 48 — criterion, light, reminder — is described in ayah 49 as landing on a particular kind of heart. Ask Allah to make yours that heart.

passages.title: Abraham confronts his people's idols
passages.tafsir:
These six ayat give us a scene from Ibrahim's life as a caller to Allah: he stands in front of his own father and his own people and asks them a question about the images they worship. The passage moves in a straight line — Allah grants Ibrahim sound judgement early on (ayah 51), Ibrahim puts his question (52), his people answer by pointing to their forefathers (53), he tells them that both they and their forefathers are in clear error (54), they ask whether he is serious (55), and he answers with the truth: your Lord is the Lord of the heavens and the earth, Who created them (56).

## A gift that came before the argument

The passage does not begin with Ibrahim speaking. It begins with Allah giving. **"And indeed, We had granted Abraham sound judgment early on"** (ayah 51). Ibn Kathir opens his comment by telling us that Allah is speaking here about **His close Friend Ibrahim, peace be upon him** — how He bestowed upon him guidance aforetime, that is, from an early age He inspired him with truth and with evidence against his people. Ibn Kathir links this to another verse, where Allah says: *"And that was Our proof which We gave Ibrahim against his people"* (6:83). The point, he says, is that Allah is telling us He gave guidance to Ibrahim aforetime — He had already guided him at an early age.

So the clarity Ibrahim uses in the next ayah is not something he manufactured for himself. It was placed in him. Where the translation says "sound judgment," Ibn Kathir renders the same word simply as **"his guidance."**

And the ayah adds, **"and We were Well-Acquainted with him."** Ibn Kathir gives this a short and beautiful gloss: it means **"he was worthy of that."** Allah knew him, and gave accordingly.

There is a quiet comfort in the order of these two ayat for anyone who worries that they are too young, or too alone, to stand for the truth. The standing came second. The gift came first.

## "What are these images?"

**"˹Remember˺ when he questioned his father and his people, 'What are these images…'"** (ayah 52). Ibn Kathir says it plainly: *this* is the guidance which he had been given during his youth — **his denunciation of his people's worship of idols instead of Allah.**

In other words, ayah 52 shows us what ayah 51 was talking about. If you want to know what "sound judgment early on" looked like in practice, it looked like a young man refusing to bow to what everyone around him bowed to.

Look at how he frames the question. He does not begin with a long argument. He asks *what are these* — he asks his people to look at the objects in front of them and say what they are. And Ibn Kathir explains the second half of the question, *"to which you are devoted,"* as meaning **"which you worship with such devotion."** That is the sting of it: the mismatch between the object and the attachment. The devotion is total; the question is whether its object can bear it.

Note also who he is addressing: **"his father and his people."** He does not begin with strangers. The first place he speaks the truth is the hardest place — his own home, his own kin.

## The one answer they had: "our fathers did it"

**"They replied, 'We found our forefathers worshipping them'"** (ayah 53). Ibn Kathir's comment is precise and quietly damning: this means **they had no other evidence apart from the misguided actions of their forefathers.**

Look at what is missing from their reply. There is no claim that the images create, or hear, or answer, or benefit. There is no argument at all. There is only a report of what they found. When a person's only reason for what they worship is that they walked in on it already happening, they have not chosen a faith; they have inherited a routine.

This is why the exchange is so useful to us. Ibrahim's question was not clever or obscure. It simply asked for a reason — and there was none to give.

## Why Ibrahim's reply cuts both ways

**"He responded, 'Indeed, you and your forefathers have been clearly astray'"** (ayah 54). His people had put their fathers between themselves and the question, as though the authority of the ancestors were a wall he could not get past. Ibrahim goes straight through it.

Ibn Kathir unpacks the logic: the meaning is that **speaking to your fathers, whose actions you cite as evidence, would be the same as speaking to you** — both you and they are misguided and are not following any straight path.

The fathers were not a separate, higher court of appeal. They were people in exactly the same position, with exactly the same absence of proof. Appealing to them changes nothing, because they had no evidence either. And the error is described as **manifest** — clear, not a subtle mistake or a fine point of dispute.

## "Are you serious, or are you playing?"

Ibn Kathir notes exactly what set off their reaction: this came **when he called their intelligence into question, and said that their fathers were misguided and belittled their gods.** Three things at once — their reasoning, their forefathers, and their objects of worship.

**"They asked, 'Have you come to us with the truth, or is this…'"** — or are you one of those who play about (ayah 55). Ibn Kathir puts their meaning like this: *"These words that you are saying, are you speaking in jest or are you telling the truth? For we have never heard such a thing before."*

That last sentence is the real content of their objection: **we have never heard such a thing before.** Notice it is not a refutation. It is astonishment dressed up as a question. The idea is so far outside anything they have encountered that their first instinct is to check whether the young man is joking. Novelty feels to them like a reason for disbelief — which is the same mistake as ayah 53 wearing different clothes. There, the old was true because it was old; here, the new is suspect because it is new. Neither is an argument.

It is worth sitting with how often serious truth is first met not with counter-evidence but with *"you can't be serious."*

## The answer: your Lord is the Lord of the heavens and the earth

**"He replied, 'In fact, your Lord is the Lord of the heavens and the earth…'"** (ayah 56). The reply opens with the word the translations render *"In fact"* and *"Nay"* — Ibrahim does not defend himself against the accusation of playing around at all. He simply states the reality, which is a far stronger answer than protesting his sincerity.

Notice that he says **your Lord** — not *my* Lord as opposed to theirs. Ibn Kathir's paraphrase puts two things side by side: **your Lord, beside Whom there is no other god, is the One Who created the heavens and the earth and all that they contain.**

And on *"Who created them,"* Ibn Kathir adds: **He is the One Who initiated their creation; He is the Creator of all things.** Set that beside the images of ayah 52. The question Ibrahim began with — *what are these?* — is answered by the description of the One he ends with.

**"And to that I am one of the witnesses."** Ibn Kathir explains that this means he bears witness that there is no true deity other than Him and no Lord except Him. They asked whether he was serious; he answers by taking the stand and putting himself on the record.

## What this passage asks of us

**Ask what a thing actually is.** Ibrahim's method in ayah 52 was not complicated. He looked at the object of devotion and asked for its identity. Anything we give ourselves to with that kind of devotion can be asked the same question.

**Inheritance is not evidence.** Ayah 53 records what Ibn Kathir calls having no other evidence apart from the misguided actions of the forefathers, and ayah 54 answers it in a line. "This is what we've always done" tells you about a habit; it does not tell you the truth of the matter. The point is not that the old is wrong, but that *"we found our forefathers doing it"* is not a reason.

**"We've never heard that before" is not a refutation.** Ayah 55 shows people treating unfamiliarity as a verdict. When we feel that reflex in ourselves, the honest move is to ask for the evidence rather than for the comfort of the familiar.

**Answer with the truth, not with self-defence.** In ayah 56 Ibrahim ignores the jab and states reality — and then bears witness to it. That is the whole shape of calling to Allah in miniature: speak the truth about the Lord of the heavens and the earth, and be willing to stand behind it.

And behind it all, ayah 51 remains: the sound judgement was **given**. Whoever wants that clarity should ask the One who granted it to Ibrahim, peace be upon him — of whom Allah said that He was Well-Acquainted with him, and, as Ibn Kathir put it, **he was worthy of that.**
